title: An Intra-Tissue Radiometry Microprobe for Measuring Radiance In Situ in Living Tissue
protocol: Mount the glass pipette by its wide end using an alligator clip, ensuring the tapered end is facing down and perpendicular to the floor.
Hang a 50 g plastic vice grip from the tapered end of the mounted glass pipette.
Place a pad of electrical tape between the pipette and the vice grip to prevent slippage.
Heat the tapered end of the pipette using a small butane torch, applying the flame 1 cm above the vice grip.
Hold the torch such that the brightest part of the flame is 3 cm from the glass, with the glass at the tip of the flame.
Trim the pulled end of the pipette once it has increased by about 5 inches.
Use scissors or a glass cutter to trim the end where the new diameter is roughly twice that of the optical fiber.
File down any sharp areas of the trimmed end using carborundum paper.
Rinse away any resulting small glass shards or dust with isopropyl alcohol followed by compressed air.
Sever the optical fiber using a razor blade, removing one SMA connector of a 200 µm diameter SMA-terminated optical fiber.
Cut the next 5 cm of plastic and fiberglass jacketing to expose the bare optical fiber.
Burn off the polyimide polymer coating from the glass fiber using a butane torch.
Rinse the exposed bare glass fiber with isopropanol.
Wipe the bare glass fiber clean using a lint-free wipe.
Mount the bare end of the optical fiber directly in a plier clamp on a table or shelf edge.
Attach two small clamps (total weight: 10 g) to the jacketed end of the fiber, about 12 inches down from where the plier clamp holds the bare fiber.
Hold the butane torch flame perpendicular to the optical fiber and 3 cm down vertically from where the plier clamp holds the bare fiber.
Allow the fiber to stretch, pull, separate, and drop to the floor.
Gently sand away any irregularities on the pulled optical fiber end with carborundum paper.
Clean the fiber with isopropyl alcohol and a lint-free wipe.
Dry the fiber with compressed air.
Darken the sides of the fiber with a film-opaquing pen to prevent stray light entry.
Insert the tapered optical fiber into the wide end of the altered glass pipette, leaving ~1 mm of bare fiber sticking out.
Secure the jacketed end of the optical fiber to the wide end of the pipette with electrical tape.
Apply a drop of cyanoacrylate adhesive onto a small-gauge needle.
Touch the drop of adhesive to the cut edge of the pulled pipette, avoiding the bare end of the pulled fiber.
Allow capillary action to wick the adhesive into the pipette and wet the area between the wall of the pipette and the optical fiber.
Allow the adhesive to cure for at least 15 min before moving the probe assembly.
Mix a drop of UV-curable adhesive with titanium dioxide powder at a 1:1 volume ratio.
Attach the probe to a micromanipulator with a mounting rod holder such that the probe is in a horizontal orientation.
Dip the tip of a wire or needle into the adhesive/TiO2 mixture prepared above to form a droplet of adhesive.
Mount the wire or needle with the droplet near the tip of the horizontal probe using an alligator clip on the bench.
Deposit a scattering sphere on the tip of the probe by slowly and carefully pushing the tip of the probe's optical fiber into the droplet of adhesive/TiO2.
Withdraw the tip from the glue quickly after each push.
Repeat steps 4 to 6 two to three times until a spherical droplet of adhesive of the desired size is deposited on the tip of the optical fiber.
Cure the sphere by connecting the SMA-terminated end of the optical fiber to a fiber-coupled UV light source.
Heat the large end of a Pasteur pipette using a butane torch.
Melt a 0.5 cm diameter hole in the bottom of a 35 mm x 10 mm plastic Petri dish with the heated pipette tip.
Seal the hole on the bottom side of the dish with electrical tape or lab tape.
Prepare liquid gelatin according to the package instructions.
Perform the dissection and preparation of the tissue that will be used.
Fill two Petri dishes from step 2.1 a quarter of the way with liquid gelatin, and let cool to room temperature just short of gelation.
Place the biopsy in the cushion of viscous gelatin that forms in the hole in the bottom of one dish.
Use a Pasteur pipette to gently add room temperature gelatin around the biopsy until the Petri dish is full.
Fill the second dish with gelatin to make a blank sample.
Place the sample dishes into a refrigerator for about 10-30 min until the gelatin is fully cured and slightly elastic to the touch.
Cut a 6 cm x 6 cm square of 1/4 inch thick plexiglass.
Drill or melt a hole in the plastic square with the same diameter as the Petri dish (~35 mm).
Ensure that the Petri dish fits snugly in this hole and is held in place with friction.
Add tape to the edges of the dish to slightly increase the size and frictional contact.
Drill or melt a 1/4 inch diameter hole in the corner of the plastic square.
Use this hole to attach the square to the micromanipulator using a 1/4 inch screw and bolt.
Cover the plastic square with black electrical tape to reduce stray light reaching the probe.
Use tape to create a skirt around the sides of the square extending below the bottom of the inserted dish (>10 mm) to reduce stray light.
Affix this micromanipulator to an optical breadboard.
Mount a collimating lens above the measurement area using a vice and frame attached to an optical breadboard.
Elevate the setup above the sample by more than 0.6 meters.
Connect a liquid light guide to the collimating lens.
Attach the other end of the liquid light guide to a broadband light source.
Secure the probe to a vertically oriented mount pointing towards the light source.
Position the probe using clamps, hose clamps, or tape on an optical table post.
Place the sample manipulator near the vertically mounted probe.
Adjust the position of the sample stage using the sample manipulator so that it is centered in the 0.5 cm opening at the bottom of the Petri dish.
Handle the setup with caution to avoid touching or bumping the tip of the mounted probe.
Prepare a boom-mounted stereomicroscope over the sample area.
View the top-down alignment of the probe tip, stage, and sample before starting an experiment.
Connect the SMA-terminated end of the probe's optical fiber to a USB fiber-optic spectrometer.
Connect the spectrometer to the computer using a USB cable.
Position the probe and manipulators in the exact aligned position for data collection.
Apply silicone lubricant to the part of the probe that will be inserted into the tissue.
Reapply silicone lubricant before each baseline or tissue measurement.
Remove the tape covering the hole in the blank sample Petri dish.
Place the Petri dish securely in the sample holder by friction.
Use the micromanipulator to lower the sample onto the probe.
Allow the probe to enter the gelatin via the hole on the underside of the petri dish.
Continue until the probe is approximately 5 mm from the bottom of the gelatin layer.
Turn on the light source.
Adjust the spectrometer integration time until the signal is as high as possible but not saturating.
Set the number of averaged scans between two and five.
Set the smoothing pixels value to six.
Collect a dark measurement.
Detach the probe fiber from the spectrometer.
Cover the port with the opaque metal cover.
Obtain a dark measurement to characterize the noise of the spectrometer with no input light.
Save this measurement according to the data acquisition strategy.
Reconnect the probe fiber to the spectrometer.
Wait for the signal to stabilize.
Acquire another spectrum characterizing the light reaching the probe through the gelatin in the absence of tissue.
Remove the tape on the bottom of the sample Petri dish.
Place the sample petri dish in the sample holder.
Align the sample dish with the probe using three-dimensional manipulation so that the tissue biopsy is centered above the tip of the probe.
Apply silicone gel to the probe.
Slowly lower the sample onto the probe until the probe tip has just entered the tissue sample.
Monitor the detected light in real-time to determine when the probe tip contacts the tissue.
Verify the integration time by ensuring the measured spectrum is neither too noisy nor saturated.
Adjust the integration time if necessary and perform a new dark measurement after any adjustment.
Take measurements and save the spectrum at each vertical position within the tissue.
Move the sample down using the micromanipulator, moving it down through five tick marks or 127 µm for each measurement.
Use spectrometer's software to convert all collected spectra to delimited text files.
Load all measurement files for a sample using Matlab or a coding language of choice.
For each tissue measurement spectrum, subtract the corresponding dark spectrum.
Divide the resulting spectrum by the integration time.
Calculate the percentage of incident light reaching each position in the tissue by dividing the spectra obtained with the probe inside the tissue by the baseline spectrum obtained in empty gelatin.
Visualize the data using contour plots.
